frictionVectors.title: European Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons while using pipeline and LNG exports to preserve leverage with Italy, Spain, and wider Europe. Long-term demand uncertainty and foreign investment requirements limit this leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Border Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Mali, Libya, and Niger increases security costs along Algeria’s southern and eastern borders. Algiers is resisting external military alignment while facing pressure to cooperate more closely with European and regional actors.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting competing US, European, Chinese, and Gulf interest because of its access to Central African copper and cobalt. Angola gains infrastructure leverage but risks becoming dependent on external capital and transit priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil Dominance
frictionVectors.details: International companies remain central to offshore production, technology, and financing despite Luanda’s efforts to strengthen national participation. Falling production and debt exposure constrain Angola’s bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Oil Export Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Benin’s control of access to the Cotonou corridor and the Niger-Benin oil pipeline has become entangled in bilateral tensions and wider regional sanctions politics. External operators and financiers retain substantial influence over the project’s commercial viability.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The port and associated logistics network remain vital to Benin’s revenue and regional trade position. Dependence on foreign construction, finance, and security partnerships creates leverage for outside powers.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is using its market importance and regulatory credibility to demand greater value capture from the diamond partnership with De Beers. The main risk is reduced investment or weaker global diamond demand rather than direct loss of sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Diversification Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are pursuing Botswana’s copper, nickel, lithium, and other mineral opportunities as the government seeks to reduce diamond dependence. Maintaining local processing and transparent licensing will determine whether diversification strengthens national control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Nationalization Drive
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over industrial and artisanal gold production, refining, and export revenues. Limited technical capacity, smuggling, and insecurity make the sector vulnerable to opaque intermediaries and external buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-Resources Risk
frictionVectors.details: Expanded ties with Russia and other non-Western partners may provide military support but can create new dependencies in mining concessions, logistics, and security contracting. Persistent jihadist attacks continue to threaten mines, roads, and electricity infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Informal Gold and Nickel Networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak regulatory capacity and opaque licensing allow domestic elites and foreign intermediaries to capture value from gold, nickel, and rare-earth prospects.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–DRC Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving Rwanda and armed groups in eastern DRC constrain Burundi's strategic autonomy and divert resources toward border security.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence on Ports and Tourism
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital and donor-backed infrastructure underpin ports, logistics, and tourism, limiting domestic leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Drought, imported fuel, and desalination costs expose the islands to external price shocks despite progress in renewable power.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, Timber, and Mining Capture
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, and emerging mining projects remain vulnerable to opaque concessions, elite rent-seeking, and unequal benefit sharing.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Driven Infrastructure Risk
frictionVectors.details: Violence in the Anglophone regions and the Far North disrupts transport corridors and weakens state control over productive zones.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security-for-Minerals Bargain
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security personnel has increased Bangui's room for maneuver against some armed groups but raises concerns over opaque access to gold and diamond networks.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and porous borders enable armed-group taxation and illicit mineral flows, leaving the state dependent on external security and logistics support.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized Oil Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and strategic autonomy remain tied to crude exports, foreign operators, and vulnerable pipeline and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: Conflict spillover from Sudan, refugee flows, and militia activity absorb state capacity and increase reliance on foreign security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a major sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' effective authority over its claimed territory and surrounding maritime resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on remittances, aid, and foreign-backed infrastructure, constraining domestic control over ports, fisheries, and energy development.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions and Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains central to global supply chains, while foreign firms and state-backed investors compete for concessions amid persistent concerns over transparency, taxation, and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east, involving M23 and broader Rwanda-linked tensions, weakens Kinshasa's control over territory, transport corridors, and mineral zones.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State finances and export capacity remain heavily tied to oil, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price shocks and the bargaining power of international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Financed Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail, and port-linked projects expand connectivity but can increase debt exposure and external influence over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Commodity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening processing and state oversight, but foreign buyers and volatile commodity markets still capture significant value from its cocoa economy.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist activity and instability in Burkina Faso and Mali place pressure on northern borders, security spending, and transport corridors linking the country to Sahelian markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: The concentration of US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates revenue but limits strategic autonomy and makes Djibouti a target during regional crises.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Port infrastructure and Ethiopia-linked trade are vital to the economy, while debt and concession exposure to foreign financiers—especially China—constrain national control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs and large Gulf-linked investments are stabilizing Egypt's finances while increasing outside influence over strategic assets, land, and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia's dam operations remain a core sovereignty and water-security concern, with negotiations unable to produce a fully binding framework for drought management.

frictionVectors.title: Declining hydrocarbon base
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil and gas fields are reducing fiscal room, leaving the state reliant on foreign operators, opaque production-sharing arrangements, and LNG-linked infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important to major public works, creating long-term repayment and strategic-dependence risks as hydrocarbon revenues weaken.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production depends on foreign partners operating under highly opaque arrangements, limiting public oversight of strategic mineral revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline is increasingly important amid regional competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, and maritime powers, raising pressure over ports and security access.

frictionVectors.title: Southern African supply-chain exposure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African transport corridors, electricity arrangements, markets, and customs systems, constraining independent control over trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and textile vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Export earnings remain exposed to changing trade preferences and external market access, while foreign-owned production limits domestic capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea access competition
frictionVectors.details: Addis Ababa's pursuit of reliable maritime access is intensifying tensions with Somalia and attracting interest from Gulf and other external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict and infrastructure fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Continued insecurity in Amhara, Oromia, and other areas disrupts transport, energy development, and resource administration, limiting federal control beyond major corridors.

highlights: Transition government seeks tighter resource control
Oil and manganese remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: Mining and oil renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing for greater local processing and state participation in manganese, oil, and timber. Investors remain wary of regulatory uncertainty during the political transition.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Transgabon railway and mineral-export corridors are strategic bottlenecks requiring foreign capital and technical support, limiting near-term sovereign leverage.

highlights: Senegal remains the critical strategic partner
Fishing and port access drive sovereignty concerns

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked security and trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional connectivity, security coordination, and access around its territory. This limits policy autonomy but reduces the risk of major external coercion.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign fleets and weak monitoring threaten domestic food security and maritime resource control. Enforcement capacity remains constrained by limited patrol assets.

highlights: Local-content push targets gold, lithium, and cocoa

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization and debt restructuring have increased external influence over economic policy. Ghana retains substantial institutional capacity but has less room to subsidize or independently develop strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and illegal extraction
frictionVectors.details: Gold and emerging lithium projects attract major foreign investment while illegal mining damages land and water resources. The government is seeking stronger local processing and bargaining power over concessions.

highlights: Junta balances China, Western firms, and state control

frictionVectors.title: Simandou external concentration
frictionVectors.details: Simandou's iron-ore development depends on large foreign-led consortia, financing, rail construction, and port infrastructure. The project may transform state revenues but risks locking Guinea into an export-focused model.

frictionVectors.title: Junta-driven regulatory uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government is demanding greater state participation while restricting political competition and civil society oversight. Uncertainty over contracts and institutional succession complicates long-term sovereign planning.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the economic lifeline
Political fragility limits resource bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Cashew dependency
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on raw cashew exports, leaving producers exposed to foreign buyers, price shocks, and limited domestic processing capacity. This weakens national control over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port, transport links, and maritime enforcement require outside support, while political instability and alleged transnational trafficking undermine state authority. Senegalese regional security influence is important but constrains autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and commercial debt pressures constrain Nairobi's policy space. Public resistance to taxation and austerity complicates efforts to preserve sovereign control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western interests compete around ports, rail, logistics, and energy corridors. Kenya is diversifying partners but remains exposed to refinancing and concessionary leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but deepen dependence on Pretoria and expose Maseru to disputes over pricing, construction, and project delays.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Sector Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: High-value diamond production remains concentrated among foreign-linked operators and is vulnerable to weak global prices and opaque beneficial ownership. Limited domestic processing reduces local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Concession Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, rubber, and forestry development rely heavily on foreign capital and long-term concessions. Weak state capacity limits Liberia's bargaining power over taxation, labor standards, and local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Freeport Strategic Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port is central to trade and external security partnerships, making logistics policy sensitive to foreign commercial and diplomatic interests. Infrastructure financing remains dependent on donors and outside operators.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and budget flows. Production remains vulnerable to blockades, force majeure threats, and factional bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Security Agendas
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain significant influence through security, migration, and energy ties. Foreign backing reinforces Libya's institutional fragmentation and limits autonomous policymaking.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains. Fiscal receipts and local processing remain limited relative to environmental and infrastructure costs.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Madagascar's island geography makes imported fuel, ports, and transport corridors strategically vulnerable. External lenders and operators hold substantial leverage over infrastructure rehabilitation and energy access.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit fiscal room and increase sensitivity to donor and creditor conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium and rare-earth projects could attract needed capital, but weak regulatory capacity risks unfavorable contracts and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state control and revenue from gold while tensions with international mining firms increase legal and operational uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-access dependency
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security assistance expands external influence while persistent insurgency threatens transport corridors, mines, and state revenue collection.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue potential but leaves Mauritania dependent on foreign operators, technology, and cross-border coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports remain tied to foreign demand and rail infrastructure, while regional insecurity and competition over logistics limit domestic bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius must balance growing Indian, Chinese, British, and American interest in maritime access, surveillance, and infrastructure around the Chagos region.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and food import exposure
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported fuel and food leaves the island vulnerable to shipping disruptions and external price shocks despite strong institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara recognition contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses infrastructure, phosphate development, and diplomatic partnerships to consolidate control, while rival claims continue to generate regional and international friction.

frictionVectors.title: Green-hydrogen dependency risk
frictionVectors.details: European investment in renewable energy and green hydrogen can accelerate industrial upgrading but may preserve external control over finance, technology, and export markets.

highlights: LNG Recovery Hindered by Cabo Delgado
Resource Wealth Still Dependent on Foreign Capital

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Security and LNG Access
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to constrain sovereign control over gas assets and surrounding infrastructure. Foreign security support remains central to protecting prospective LNG operations.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing and Port Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and dependence on foreign investors limit Maputo's bargaining power over major ports, energy corridors, and extractive projects.

highlights: Oil and Green Hydrogen Reshape Strategic Leverage
Strong Institutions Guard Resource Bargaining Power

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Licensing and Revenue Control
frictionVectors.details: New offshore discoveries are attracting major international energy companies, creating pressure to secure better local participation, fiscal terms, and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen proposals could diversify the economy, but foreign financing, land access, and water use may constrain domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control over uranium and other mineral assets while reducing reliance on former colonial partners. Regulatory confrontation risks investment withdrawal and operational disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on cross-border pipelines and insecure transport routes limits the practical value of expanding national control over oil production.

highlights: Oil Theft and Grid Weakness Dilute Gains

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: The state continues to lose production and revenue through theft, vandalism, and weak enforcement in the Niger Delta. This undermines control even as reforms seek to improve sector governance.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Production-Sharing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain important for deepwater production and technical capacity, limiting Abuja's ability to capture the full value of its hydrocarbon reserves.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Minerals and Conflict Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Allegations linking Rwanda to armed groups and mineral flows in eastern Congo create sustained diplomatic pressure and threaten regional supply-chain legitimacy.

frictionVectors.title: Aid, Investment, and Strategic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Kigali maintains strong administrative control, but dependence on external aid, investment, and security partnerships constrains fully autonomous economic policymaking.

highlights: Maritime diplomacy over Gulf of Guinea resources

frictionVectors.title: Offshore hydrocarbons uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Unproven oil prospects continue to attract external interest, but limited exploration and weak domestic capacity constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's control over potential resources.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, connectivity, and energy projects rely heavily on foreign finance and technical assistance, creating modest exposure to competing Portuguese, Chinese, and other outside interests.

highlights: Oil and gas revenues test fiscal independence

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-operated hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil and gas production offers major revenue potential, but international operators, financing structures, and contract terms remain central to Senegal's ability to capture value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure constraints
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal pressure limits Dakar's room to renegotiate projects or expand state participation, increasing dependence on lenders and external investors for energy and transport infrastructure.

highlights: Blue economy remains a sovereignty pillar

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from licensing and tuna-related activity but faces persistent challenges in monitoring distant-water fleets and ensuring that foreign access produces durable domestic value.

frictionVectors.title: Competing strategic partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf engagement in maritime security, ports, and infrastructure offers leverage but can narrow policy autonomy in a strategically important archipelago.

highlights: Mining reform collides with foreign capital needs

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining value chains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and gold projects remain heavily dependent on foreign operators and export infrastructure, limiting domestic capture of processing, logistics, and revenue value.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-resources exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large mining investments can improve roads, ports, and power access, but opaque or highly concessionary arrangements risk converting infrastructure needs into long-term external leverage.

highlights: Ports and security partnerships shape sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil and maritime claims
frictionVectors.details: Exploration and licensing ambitions are constrained by insecurity, federal-regional disputes, and contested maritime interests, leaving Somalia vulnerable to unfavorable external terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Gulf, and other external partners provide essential security, port, and logistics support, but dependence complicates unified national control over maritime assets and commercial corridors.

highlights: Energy and logistics reform remain decisive

frictionVectors.title: POWER AND PORT BOTTLENECKS
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity, rail and port constraints weaken South Africa's ability to capture value from minerals and agricultural exports. State reforms and private investment are improving resilience, but implementation remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS INVESTMENT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European states, China and Gulf investors are competing for access to lithium, manganese, platinum-group metals and other strategic resources. Pretoria is seeking downstream beneficiation while avoiding excessive dependence on any single partner.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the sovereignty bottleneck

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE THROUGH SUDAN
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving production, transit fees and fiscal revenues vulnerable to disruption. Foreign operators and neighboring governments retain substantial leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: ELITE CONTROL OF RESOURCE FLOWS
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions, delayed political transition and competition among armed-political networks limit transparent control of oil income. External security and commercial partners can secure access without materially strengthening broad-based state capacity.

highlights: War fragments control of strategic assets
Gold and ports attract external competition

frictionVectors.title: RED SEA AND PORT SOVEREIGNTY
frictionVectors.details: The conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces has made control of Port Sudan and associated corridors strategically vital. Regional and extra-regional actors are seeking influence over logistics, military access and future reconstruction.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling networks provide finance to armed actors and attract competing foreign buyers. Fragmented authority prevents the state from exercising reliable control over extraction, taxation and export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The expansion of Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port infrastructure is increasing Tanzania's leverage over regional trade, while foreign lenders, contractors and neighboring states gain long-term influence. The government is balancing access with tighter control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND LNG BARGAINING
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking greater local participation and fiscal returns from gold, critical minerals and prospective LNG development. Negotiations with multinational firms create investment opportunities but also recurring disputes over taxation, ownership and environmental obligations.

highlights: Lome remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lome strengthens Togo's role as a coastal gateway for the Sahel, but its expansion depends on foreign finance, operators and external trade networks. This creates leverage for outside commercial powers over customs, logistics and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN BORDER INSECURITY
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the central Sahel is increasing pressure on northern communities and transport routes. Expanded security cooperation with external partners may protect corridors but can narrow domestic policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and migration cooperation provide Tunis with essential fiscal and political support while increasing outside leverage over domestic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate and Energy Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Declining phosphate output, electricity subsidies, and reliance on imported energy limit Tunisia's control over strategic revenue and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Risk
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to export ambitions but faces Western legal, environmental, and financing pressure, increasing dependence on non-Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and lenders retain a major role in roads, power, and oil infrastructure, creating long-term exposure to foreign contractors and repayment obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors are competing for copper and cobalt access, giving Zambia leverage but also risking weak local processing and limited value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Constraints
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and debt restructuring improve fiscal space, while external financing conditions continue to shape mining, energy, and transport policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors dominate much of the lithium and platinum investment pipeline, while domestic processing requirements remain difficult to enforce.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted market access, and chronic currency instability push Harare toward opaque bilateral financing and resource-backed arrangements with external partners.
